title: David-Horodok’s fires brought the town together to build a brigade
summary: Repeated fires were serious enough to prompt residents to establish a firefighters’ association, making communal self-organization part of town life.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Founding of the David-Horodok Firefighters Association

editorialContent:
![David-Horodok on the Horyn River](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg/1920px-%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%8B%D0%B4-%D0%93%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BA%2C_%D1%86%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA%D0%B2%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%B0%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D1%96%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%8B_%D0%91%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%86%D1%96.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)
## A town that prepared for fire

In David-Horodok, fire was not a distant danger but a recurring threat to ordinary life. The memorial book, in JewishGen’s translation, describes a town of wooden houses and thatched roofs where fire could return “almost every summer.” A hot iron left outside, a torch carried to a stable at night, an unextinguished cigarette, children playing with fire—or arson—could set a blaze in motion. Wind and closely packed combustible roofs could turn a mishap into a catastrophe. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav375.html))

Summer was a season of beauty and activity, but the danger changed how families lived. Some carried valuables to the town’s few brick houses; others kept belongings packed for a quick escape. One recollection makes the threat part of family chronology: the narrator’s mother used [the Great Fire](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_ffaa51036bca0a86af298030) to mark the time of his birth. The passage does not give a year, so it cannot securely identify that fire with the later blaze of 1936.

Another memory reaches further back. The [head of the kahal](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_ff9dd6d63a16afd17ca4405b) reportedly recalled a substantial fire in 1868. The memorial book presents community inquiries into the Great Fire’s date, but the evidence supplied here does not settle when it occurred. These accounts preserve how fires served as markers in local memory without allowing us to make one event out of every remembered blaze. The town stood in [Polesia](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a6cfefdf02483d0a9aecb8d6), a region whose wooded landscape and small settlements formed the wider setting of life, but the book’s account is specifically about the hazards faced in David-Horodok.

## Founders and a shared undertaking

After numerous fires, residents organized a formal response. The memorial book dates the [David-Horodok Firefighters Association](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1a77e56df6486c4ebcd2b349)’s founding to 1904; the separate event record gives the same year. The organization was not the work of one community alone. Jewish founders named in the book include Zeev Yudovitz and his son Bezalel, Mordecai (Moche) Rimer, Nisan Gorvitz, and Liba Fridman. The non-Jewish founders included Captain Tzereiski and Petrushkevitz. Tzereiski became the first commander and Petrushkevitz the secretary. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

The first contribution was practical and immediate: Zeev Yudovitz gave the organization his private well and two barrels. Jewish and non-Jewish residents also donated, and an insurance society in Minsk provided money for equipment. The account makes the brigade an example of shared local self-protection: fires threatened the whole town, and the response drew on residents and institutions beyond one household or group.

The memorial book names the people behind the association, but it does not explain all their family connections. It identifies Bezalel as Zeev’s son, for example, and lists Rimer and Gorvitz among the founders; it does not establish whether every similarly named person in other records belongs to these same families. The book also notes that Zeev built the Great Study House, but the brief evidence here does not show that this civic role and his firefighting contribution were part of the same undertaking.

## Equipment, training, and public life

The organization grew from donated water and barrels into a lasting civic institution. In 1911–1912, when Tzereiski was sent to the front, Rimer took command, assisted by Bezalel Yudovitz and Nisan Gorvitz. In 1919, the book says, Bezalel was murdered and Gorvitz became ill; Yosef Yudovitz and Simcha Mishalov replaced them. Petrushkevitz remained secretary until 1920, when Aharon Moravchik took over. These changes show how the brigade depended on successive local leaders, even as war and personal loss affected its ranks. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

By the time the Poles entered in 1920, the association had five pumps and eighteen barrels, along with other equipment. During the Polish period, two benzene motors and long rubber hoses were added. Its building grew, and a theater shared the premises; its proceeds helped fund firefighting. In 1937 a 25-meter tower with a siren was erected beside it. When an alarm sounded, 35 wagon drivers were summoned with their horses to carry people and equipment. The memorial book counts 63 volunteer firefighters, ten of them Poles. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

Training became a public ritual as well as preparation. In summer, the station watchman Massey walked the streets sounding a special bugle. Firefighters gathered in uniform, exercised, and staged a mock blaze at a house selected by one of their number. The recollection even preserves the drill’s comic edge: sometimes they chose the home of someone against whom they held a grudge. The townspeople watched; afterward, the firefighters shared beer. Such details make visible the association’s place in everyday life—not only as emergency equipment, but as a body of young people who practiced together and were recognized by their neighbors.

## The 1936 fire—and the limits of the defense

After the First World War, the brigade expanded. The town council increased its equipment and supported instruction in extinguishing fires and, especially, preventing them from spreading. The memorial book’s account of everyday life says almost all Jewish young people enrolled, regarding service as a civic obligation. Yet it also notes a disparity: although Christian residents’ thatched roofs faced particular danger, only three or four Christians joined the brigade. A separate account emphasizes that the fire department served the whole town and was the only Jewish-operated institution to receive a municipal subsidy. Together, these recollections show both broad community service and uneven participation. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav375.html))

The limits of the brigade became clear in 1936. According to the memorial book, a fire broke out in the middle of the day in the Christian part of town. Wind and nearby thatched roofs helped it spread beyond the firefighters’ ability to contain it. One account says one third of the town burned, including the Greek Orthodox church on the hill. Another memorial-book passage labels an image “The large fire of 1936 in David-Horodok.” These are accounts of the same dated catastrophe, but the supplied evidence does not give a more exact count of destroyed homes or independently verify the fraction of the town lost. The fire was a disaster, not proof that the association had failed: the book records both the brigade’s extensive preparations and the conditions under which it could not stop a blaze. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav103.html))

The memorial book carries the brigade’s story into the years before the Second World War. In 1935, command passed from the aging Rimer to Simcha Mishalov; in 1937 Yosef Kozak replaced Mishalov, assisted by Yosef Yudovitz, Mishalov, and Yaakov Matosvitz. The association continued until the Red Army entered. By 1938 it had financed a brick theater, replacing an earlier wooden one, and its firefighters sometimes traveled to extinguish fires in nearby villages. The alarm tower, volunteers, wagons, pumps, theater, and shared donations tell one story: recurring danger pushed residents to build an organized response, while the 1936 blaze showed that collective effort could reduce vulnerability without mastering fire.

The independent record is thinner on this particular story. Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos identifies David-Horodok under the names Dawidgródek, Davyd-Haradok, and David-Gorodok, but its entry does not discuss the fire brigade or the 1936 fire. Virtual Shtetl’s town page confirms the place and its variant names, but likewise adds no independent account of the association or blaze. I found no relevant fire-brigade account in the searched YIVO or USHMM results. Thus the brigade’s founding, named organizers, equipment, and great fire remain documented here through the community’s own memorial book, not independently corroborated by those archives. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224))
